Seats, Usage or Outcomes

Playbooklowob research

By Chris WellsFrom lowob RESEARCH · 29 April 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 12-minute read · Revenue

Pick the pricing model that matches how value shows up, know your cost per task, and report the eight numbers that show whether the business works. Seats fit when a named person uses the product daily; usage fits when value scales with volume; outcomes fit when both sides trust the measurement. Most AI companies now land on a hybrid: Kyle Poyar's 2026 survey of 230 software companies found 37% use one, up from 25% a year earlier. Whatever the model, a price set without a known cost per task is a guess.

This page is the hub of lowob's pricing library. Each model has its own explainer: seat-based pricing, usage-based pricing and outcome-based pricing. The cost side is covered in what AI inference cost is, and the logic behind charging for results in value-based pricing. This piece is where they meet: which model to choose, what it costs to serve, and how to write the contract.

Three models and the fit test

There are three ways to charge for an AI product. Each fits a specific situation, and forcing the wrong one creates friction with buyers and finance teams.

ModelFits whenWatch for
SeatsA named human uses it daily and the value is their timeUsage spread across few heavy users
UsageValue scales with volume and the buyer accepts variable billsBill shock, procurement blocking variable spend
OutcomesYou can measure the result and the buyer trusts the measurementDisputes over attribution

Seats work when the product sits in a person's daily workflow. The buyer understands the model and can budget for it. The weakness is that AI products often do the work of several people. Seat pricing then undercharges.

Usage pricing matches value to volume. It fits products that process documents, tickets, calls or records. Buyers accept it only with caps, estimates and alerts. Without them, finance will not sign.

Outcome pricing is the most attractive and the hardest to run. You need a result you can measure, and a buyer who accepts your measurement. Resolved tickets, qualified leads, completed filings. If either side can argue about the number, the model breaks.

What the market charges

Prices below were checked on the vendors' own pages on 16 November 2026, in US dollars.

Vendor and productModelPublished priceDetail that matters
Microsoft 365 Copilot BusinessSeat, with metered extras$21 per user per month on annual billing; $25.20 monthlyPromotional $18 for the first year, 1 July to 31 December 2026. Some advanced features bill through Copilot Credits
Salesforce Agentforce add-onsSeat (unmetered)$125 per user per monthSales, Service, Field Service and Operations; Industries add-ons $150
Salesforce Flex CreditsUsage (prepaid credits)$500 per 100,000 creditsSalesforce prices each action at $0.10
Salesforce ConversationsUsage (per conversation)$2 per conversationThe original Agentforce unit, regardless of task complexity
Intercom FinOutcomeFrom $0.99 per Fin outcomeCharged at most once per conversation; no seats needed for Fin alone
Zendesk AI agentsOutcome, with an allowanceNot published; through sales5 to 15 automated resolutions per agent per month included, by plan

Salesforce is the clearest case: the same agent can be bought per user, per conversation or per action. Its own example puts a three-to-six action sales interaction at $0.30 to $0.60 under Flex Credits, against $2 per conversation.

The table also shows why seat pricing undercharges for agents. One $125 seat covers a person supervising an agent. If that agent handles 2,000 conversations a month, the vendor collects $125 for work that would bill at $4,000 on Salesforce's own $2 per-conversation meter. Our piece on which AI assistant to buy and for which seats covers the buyer's side of the same arithmetic.

How pricing is shifting: the evidence

Four recent surveys point the same way, with a caveat on outcomes. All are run by investors, analysts or newsletter authors, not audited market data, and their samples differ.

PublisherSample and dateFinding
Kyle Poyar, Growth Unhinged230 B2B software and AI companies, April to May 202637% use a hybrid model, up from 25%; 29% offer AI credits and 33% plan to within 6 to 12 months; three in four changed pricing or packaging in the past year
ICONIQ (investor), January 2026 snapshotAbout 300 executives at AI software companiesOutcome-based pricing at 18%, up from 2% in Q2 2025; 37% plan to change their AI pricing model within a year
ICONIQ (investor), State of AI, July 2026About 300 executives, Q2 2026 surveyConsumption-based pricing rose from 35% to 42% and outcome-based from 18% to 23% in six months; companies blend an average of 1.7 models
The Futurum Group (analyst)830 IT decision makers, 1H 2026For GenAI features, 42.9% of buyers prefer consumption pricing; preference for outcome-based GenAI pricing fell from 30.9% to 26.8%

Sellers' and buyers' data diverge on outcomes: more vendors offer outcome pricing while fewer buyers say they prefer it for AI features. Futurum's analyst read this as a case for hybrids, with stable subscriptions for the platform and transparent metering for AI. That matches lowob's view. Outcome pricing is easier in a pitch than in a contract, because the buyer has to accept the seller's count.

If either side can argue about the number, the model breaks.

Hybrids are normal

Most AI companies land on a hybrid. A platform fee plus usage. Seats with a usage allowance and overage. A base fee with an outcome bonus.

Hybrids are fine as long as they are simple to explain in one sentence. If your pricing page needs a calculator, buyers will assume the worst case.

The platform fee covers your fixed cost of serving a customer. The variable part tracks inference. That split keeps gross margin predictable even when usage swings.

Hybrid structurePublished exampleWhat the variable part tracksMain risk
Seat plus metered extrasMicrosoft 365 Copilot BusinessAdvanced features and custom agents, in Copilot CreditsMetered spend nobody budgeted for
Seat plus included allowance plus overageZendesk Suite, with 5 to 15 automated resolutions per agent includedResolutions above the allowance, billed monthlyAllowance expiring unused at year end
Seats plus per-outcome feeIntercom seats from $19 to $132 per seat, plus Fin from $0.99 per outcomeFin outcomesDisputes over what counts as an outcome
Prepaid credits with drawdownSalesforce Flex CreditsActions drawn down from the prepaid creditsCredit burn rate faster than forecast
Platform fee plus graduated usageLangfuse Pro: $199 a month, then $8 per 100,000 units falling to $6 at volumeVolume above an included tier, at falling unit ratesTier boundaries that create cliff edges

The one-sentence test applies to every row. "Each seat includes ten AI resolutions a month, and extras are billed monthly at the rate on your order form" passes.

The gross-margin trap

Every AI pricing model fails in the same way: the company does not know what a task costs to run.

Cost per task is model cost plus compute plus any human review, divided by tasks completed. If you cannot produce that number for last month, you do not know your gross margin. Pricing decisions made without it are guesses.

The trap is real at the industry level. ICONIQ's July 2026 report puts average AI product gross margins at 45% in 2025, projected at 53% for 2026, and notes that inference takes a growing share of cost as products scale. A margin that low leaves little room for a pricing model that misreads cost.

A worked example

The example below is illustrative. It prices an AI support agent sold at $0.99 per resolution, the entry rate Intercom lists for Fin, and runs it on a mid-tier model at Anthropic's published Claude Sonnet 5.5 rates of $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens and $0.10 per million cached input tokens (checked 16 November 2026). Intercom renamed itself Fin in May 2026, and on 15 June 2026 Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire it for about $3.6 billion.

LineHealthy monthDrifted month
Model calls per conversation44
Tokens per call6,000 input (5,000 cached), 400 output6,000 input (none cached), 400 output
Model cost per call$0.0065$0.016
Model cost per conversation$0.026$0.064
Retrieval, tools and compute per conversation (assumed)$0.010$0.010
Human review: share of conversations checked, at 2 minutes and $40 an hour10%, so $0.13320%, so $0.267
Total cost per conversation$0.169$0.341
Resolution rate (only resolutions bill)60%40%
Cost per resolution$0.28$0.85
Gross margin at $0.9971.5%14.0%

Human review costs about five times the model in the healthy month, so a cost per task that leaves out people misses most of the cost. Caching alone more than halves model cost. And the resolution rate is the denominator: when fewer conversations resolve, every cost is spread over fewer billable outcomes. Under outcome pricing the drift shows up in the margin within the month.

The number must be falling. Caching repeated context, routing simple tasks to smaller models, shortening prompts, batching requests. Each one is an operating project with an owner and a target. Anthropic's published rates show the scale: its smallest current model lists at $0.10 per million input tokens against $2 for the mid-tier model, and the Batch API halves both input and output prices. Our piece on raising for an AI company covered why investors ask for this. Here it is the difference between a business and a hobby. The token explainer shows how to estimate the inputs.

Set a margin floor per task and price above it. If a customer's usage pattern drops below the floor, you need to know within the month, not at renewal.

Free tiers are acquisition cost

A free tier is a marketing expense that happens to look like a product. Treat it that way.

Every free task has an inference cost. Add those up by month and you have a number to put next to paid channels. If free-tier conversion to paid is weak, the free tier is an expensive campaign with no stop date.

Do not count free users as users in any report that goes to the board or to investors. Count them as a channel with a cost per acquired team, and compare that cost to the others.

Contract terms that protect both sides

Variable pricing moves risk into the contract. The large vendors' published terms show which clauses matter.

TermWhat it settlesPublished precedentBuyer asks forSeller needs
Outcome definitionWhat counts as a billable resultIntercom bills resolutions, procedure handoffs, qualifications and disqualifications; a customer asking for a human is not billedA written definition and a list of exclusionsA definition it can count automatically
Verification methodHow a result is confirmedZendesk uses an LLM to check each conversation; those that fail do not consume a resolutionAccess to the evidence behind each chargeAgreement that its method is the count
Counting windowWhen a result is finalZendesk evaluates email conversations 72 hours after the first email, messaging after 2 hours by defaultA window long enough for reopened cases to surfaceA window short enough to bill monthly
Charge limit per interactionStops double countingIntercom charges at most once per conversationThe same, in the order formClarity on what a conversation is
Allowance and expiryWhether unused volume carries overZendesk allocations expire annually or at term end, capped at 10,000 a yearRollover, or a lower commitmentCommitment it can plan capacity around
Overage rate and billingPrice beyond the commitmentZendesk bills overage monthly, at a higher rate than committed usageA capped overage rate and alerts at set thresholdsThe right to bill monthly
Spend cap or pauseProtection from bill shockZendesk lets accounts pause AI features at the limit or pay overage as they goA hard cap optionNotice before a cap stops service
True-upReconciling commitment with actual usePractice varies; not on the public pages checkedCredit for under-use against renewalPayment for over-use at an agreed rate
Metric change noticeProtection when the unit changesIntercom moved from resolutions to outcomes on 12 March 2026 after emailing customers in February; Zendesk gives 30 days' notice of plan movesNotice, and the old unit until renewalThe ability to evolve the product

The Intercom change is the one to study. Its billable unit now includes some procedure handoffs to a human or a workflow, which a buyer might not call an outcome. That is why the definition belongs in the contract, not on a help page that can change. For the buyer's side of outcome deals, see what outcome-based pricing for AI is; for credit deals, usage-based pricing.

What to report, and what to stop

Our piece Stop reporting reach made the case for activation, retention, revenue, efficiency and source over reach. For an AI product those become eight monthly numbers.

NumberDefinition
ActivationShare of new teams that complete a first real task within a week
Weekly active teamsTeams, not individuals
Tasks completedThe unit of value delivered, defined once and not changed
Retention at 30 and 90 daysMeasured on teams that activated
Net revenue retentionWhat last year's customers are paying now
Gross marginNet of inference, with the trend
Cost per taskModel, compute and human review over tasks completed
Cost per acquired team by sourceWith the free tier shown as a source

Stop reporting sign-ups, which measure a landing page. Stop reporting prompts sent, which measure curiosity. Stop reporting anything counted as "AI-generated". None of them tells you whether the product works or whether the business does.

Pricing changes as experiments

Pricing is not set once. It is changed in small steps, each run as an experiment.

Write down the hypothesis, the segment it applies to, the number you expect to move and the stop rule. A stop rule is the condition under which you revert. Activation falls by a set amount, or churn rises, or support tickets about billing double.

Run it on new customers first. Existing customers get grandfathered until the result is in. Then decide, record the decision, and move on to the next one. Our guide to pricing experiments in B2B covers how to read results at low volume.

lowob takeaways

  • Run the fit test first. Seat pricing often undercharges because AI products can do the work of several people.
  • Know the cost per task. Model cost plus compute plus human review, divided by tasks completed, and it must fall.
  • Write the outcome into the contract. Definition, verification, counting window and change notice, not a help-centre link.
  • Keep hybrids to one sentence. If the pricing page needs a calculator, buyers will assume the worst case.
  • Report eight numbers. Stop reporting sign-ups, prompts sent and anything counted as AI-generated.
Gateway card

Before you publish a price

  • Pricing model chosen against the fit test, explained in one sentence
  • Cost per task known for last month, including human review, with a reduction target and an owner
  • Margin floor per task set, with alerts when a customer drops below it
  • Outcome or usage unit defined in the contract, with exclusions and a counting window
  • Overage rate, cap option and true-up terms written down
  • Free tier costed and reported as an acquisition channel
  • The eight monthly numbers on one page, sign-ups and prompt counts removed
  • Next pricing experiment written down with a stop rule

Common questions

Should I price my AI product per seat or by usage?

Seats fit when a named person uses it daily and the value is their time. Usage fits when value scales with volume and the buyer accepts variable bills, provided you offer caps, estimates and alerts. Many vendors now combine both.

How do you calculate cost per task for an AI product?

Add model cost, compute and any human review for the month, then divide by tasks completed. Include review: in our illustrative support example it cost about five times more than the model.

What is outcome-based pricing for AI, and how much does it cost?

The buyer pays per defined result, such as a resolved ticket. Intercom lists Fin from $0.99 per outcome, charged at most once per conversation, as checked in November 2026. The contract must define what counts.

What is hybrid pricing for AI products?

A fixed part, such as a platform fee or seats, plus a variable part tied to usage or outcomes. Kyle Poyar's 2026 survey found 37% of software companies use one, up from 25% a year earlier.

Next move

Work out last month's cost per task, including the people who review the AI's work, and divide your price by it. If the margin is below your floor for any customer segment, write down one cost-reduction project with an owner and one pricing experiment with a stop rule this week.
